properties.summary: A knowledge-graph agent that ingests URLs, pasted text and uploaded files, extracts entities into a graph, and answers questions over that graph instead of over raw text.
The async Python web framework the service runs on. It serves the REST API under /api, the WebSocket endpoint at /ws/graph, and the single-page frontend at the root path.
The graph database holding every extracted entity as an :Entity node and every relationship as a :RELATES_TO edge, with the semantic relationship name kept in a property.

The retrieval pipeline: vector search first when a semantic embedding is available, then keyword search, then a two-hop neighbourhood walk, and finally an LLM answer grounded only in that graph context.
A submit-then-track queue. A request returns a queued job record immediately while two background workers execute the ingest and report each stage back to the caller.
The in-memory registry behind the queue. It tracks job state, caps concurrency, evicts old finished jobs, and drains everything still in flight at shutdown.
The live push channel at /ws/graph. It emits job_update, graph_update and graph_merge messages so every connected browser sees the graph change as it is written.
The force-directed visualisation in the browser. Nodes are coloured by entity type and merged nodes are removed in place rather than through a full redraw.
The single-page UI: ingest controls, a question box, a source list, and the graph canvas. Every dynamic value is escaped before it reaches the DOM because scraped content is untrusted.
The fetch-time protection around URL ingestion: only http and https, every DNS record checked against private ranges, redirects re-validated by hand, a streamed size cap and a content-type gate.
Fetches a page, strips scripts, navigation and boilerplate, and hands clean text plus a title downstream. The title becomes the document identity for provenance.
Accepts an uploaded document, parses the bytes into plain text, rejects unparseable files up front, and then joins the same extract-and-write tail as URL ingestion.
Asks the language model for a strict JSON envelope of nodes and edges, using a fixed entity vocabulary of Person, Org, Concept, Event, Place and Technology.
Prefixes every node id with a hash of its source document so two documents never collide, drops edges pointing at ids that were never declared, and writes nodes and edges in one transaction.
A 384-dimension cosine vector index over entity embeddings. Only genuinely semantic vectors are trusted for retrieval; deterministic stand-in vectors are excluded.
The retrieval path that works with no embedding service at all: the question is stripped of stopwords and each surviving term is matched as a substring against entity labels, aliases and summaries.
One node label carrying id, label, type, summary, a normalised label, a list of source documents, aliases, and an embedding with the method that produced it.
Lowercase, strip punctuation, collapse whitespace. The normalised form is what turns spelling variants of the same entity into a detectable duplicate group.
Suggest-only by design. Exact normalised-label matches across different documents are proposed, and a human confirms the merge that repoints edges and unions provenance.
The decentralised GPU network the project calls for embeddings. When no endpoint is configured the embedding step degrades to a deterministic local vector instead of failing.
The rule that every external service has a local fallback, so the whole application boots and demos correctly with zero configured keys and reports which path actually ran.
A per-IP in-memory limit of ten requests a minute shared across the ingest and ask routes, sitting in front of everything expensive.

properties.summary: The four HackSprint sponsors GraphAgent Forge integrates: Daytona, Nosana, Neo4j and Kimi AI. Three of the four sponsors provide a service with a local fallback, so the app still runs when nothing is configured.

Sandbox-execution sponsor. Among the sponsors that provide compute, Daytona provides ephemeral sandboxes used to verify each freshly ingested subgraph; with no API key the same check provides a local subprocess instead.

Decentralised GPU sponsor. Of the four sponsors, Nosana provides the embedding endpoint that makes semantic retrieval possible; unconfigured, the client provides a deterministic hash vector so nothing crashes.

Graph-database sponsor. Neo4j provides the managed Aura instance the knowledge graph lives in; it is the one dependency the sponsors provide that has no offline substitute, so the app boots degraded without it.

Language-model sponsor. Kimi provides both entity extraction and the grounded answer step; unlike the other sponsors it deliberately provides no fallback, returning a structured error when its key is missing.
The research company behind the Kimi model family. It publishes the OpenAI-compatible endpoint the project talks to and sets the model identifier read from configuration.
The client used to spin up an ephemeral sandbox and run the graph-integrity check inside it. The graph payload is piped over standard input rather than embedded in the command line.
The stand-in for sandboxed execution: the same verification script runs in a local subprocess with a thirty-second timeout, and the result records which path was taken.
The configured embedding service. Vectors that come back non-finite are rejected outright rather than written into the index.
A deterministic 384-dimension unit-norm vector derived from the text itself. It keeps the write path working, but it carries no semantic signal, so retrieval must not treat it as one.
The blockchain the GPU marketplace settles on. Jobs submitted to the network are paid and accounted for there.
The managed graph database service holding entities, relationships, the normalised-label index and the cosine vector index.
The long-context model used for both extraction and answering. Its identifier comes from configuration and is resolved in exactly one place.
A missing model key produces a plain JSON error object that travels through the pipeline as data, never an SDK exception escaping into a 500.
The configuration in which the application is demonstrated with no API keys at all: seeded graph data, keyword retrieval, local verification and deterministic vectors.
The recorded provenance of every stored vector. Retrieval and duplicate suggestion both read it to decide whether a vector is trustworthy enough to reason from.
